opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite parts of that work, partly because addition seems so simple that you'd think there's nothing interesting to find, and it turns out there's quite a lot.

When we look at a single prompt, say "36 plus 59," with an attribution graph, we see the model isn't doing the carry-the-one algorithm you learned in school. It runs a few pathways in parallel. One is low precision and handles magnitude: roughly 36 plus roughly 60 lands somewhere around 90-something. Another is high precision but narrow: it only cares about the last digits, so a 6 plus a 9 ends in a 5. Those two get combined at the end, and you get 95.

But a single prompt only tells you what happened that one time. You want to know whether this is a general mechanism or a one-off trick. That's where the global-weights view helps. Instead of asking what fired on this input, you look at how features connect through the weights themselves, independent of any particular prompt. When you do that for the addition features, you see a very regular structure. There are operand features that respond to something like "the first number ends in 6" or "the number is around 30." Those feed into what we started calling lookup-table features, which respond to pairs, like "something ending in 6 plus something ending in 9." Those in turn feed sum features, like "the answer ends in 5" or "the answer is in the 90s." When you lay out those connections, you can see the arithmetic in the weights. The connections line up with modular patterns and with the magnitude bands you'd expect.

The bit I find most striking is the reuse. Those same lookup-table features show up in places that don't look like an addition problem at all. If the model is working out the end year of something that started in one year and lasted a certain number of years, or filling in a column in a table, or dealing with numbers in a citation, the same circuitry lights up. So it isn't memorizing "36 plus 59 equals 95" as a fact. It has built a fairly general piece of machinery and routes many different tasks through it. The global weights let you see that generality directly instead of inferring it from a pile of examples.

And there's a fun coda. If you ask Claude how it did the sum, it'll tell you it carried the one, the standard textbook explanation. That isn't what the circuits show. It learned to explain arithmetic by imitating how humans describe it, and separately learned to do arithmetic its own way. That gap between what a model says it's doing and what it's actually doing is a big reason we think this kind of tooling matters.

I'd add a caveat, too. These are replacement-model approximations. We're looking at features in a transcoder that stands in for the real MLPs, and there's error we can't always account for. So I'd call it a strong, consistent picture rather than a complete proof. But the fact that the per-prompt graphs and the global weights tell the same story gives me a lot more confidence that it's real.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a single-prompt attribution graph with global weights that show how features connect independently of a particular prompt.

r002.rationale: It describes operand features feeding shared lookup-table and sum features, and says this machinery handles addition generally rather than memorizing one sum.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favorite parts of that work, because it's where you really see the difference between looking at a single prompt and looking at the model as a whole.

So to back up a bit: in the circuit tracing paper, most of what we show are attribution graphs. You take a specific prompt, say "36 plus 59 equals," and you trace how features activate and flow into each other to produce "95." And for that one prompt, you see this really pretty structure. There's a set of features that are sort of fuzzy lookup table features, so things like "the first operand is in the mid-thirties," "the second operand ends in a nine," and then there are features that encode the sum modulo ten, and features that encode a rough magnitude of the answer, and those get combined into the output. It looks a lot like the model is doing two parallel computations, one approximate and one exact on the last digit, and then intersecting them.

But the natural worry is, okay, is that just what happened on this one prompt? Maybe for 47 plus 28 the model does something totally different. And the attribution graph alone can't tell you that, because it's a local picture, it's specific to that input.

That's where the global weights come in. The replacement model we trained, the cross-layer transcoder, has actual weights connecting features to each other, independent of any prompt. So instead of asking "what fired here," you can ask "what does this feature structurally promote or suppress, across all contexts." And when we did that for the addition features, the picture was really striking. If you take a feature like "the sum has a ones digit of five," and you look at which input features have strong positive weights into it, you get exactly the pairs of operand features you'd expect: things ending in six combined with things ending in nine, things ending in seven combined with things ending in eight, and so on. So the lookup table structure isn't something we constructed by picking a prompt. It's sitting there in the weights.

And the part I find most compelling is you can visualize it. If you plot a feature's activation or its downstream weight as a function of the two operands, so a hundred by hundred grid, you see these diagonal stripes and these periodic patterns, and those patterns are basically the geometry of addition. The modular features show up as diagonals with period ten. The magnitude features show up as these broad bands. So the shared structure is that the same small set of mechanisms, the fuzzy lookup, the mod-ten features, the magnitude features, is being reused across the whole space of two-digit problems, and the global weights let you confirm that rather than just hope for it.

The caveat I'd always add is that the replacement model is an approximation. These weights are the weights of the transcoder, not literally the weights of Claude, and there's error that we account for separately. But the fact that the local story from one prompt and the global story from the weights line up so well is what gave us confidence that we were looking at a real, general algorithm and not an artifact of one example.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts prompt-specific attribution graphs with transcoder weights that show feature connections independently of a particular prompt and across contexts.

r002.rationale: It says the same small set of addition mechanisms is reused across the full space of two-digit problems, and describes this as evidence for a general algorithm, while noting the transcoder is an approximation.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is between the structure the model has learned and the parts of that structure it uses for a particular problem. In the circuit-tracing analysis, the replacement model’s weights are shared across prompts, while the feature activations depend on the input. So two addition problems can activate different features while still using overlapping computational pathways.

That gives us a way to look for reusable structure: are similar numerical features connected in similar ways across examples? And where do the pathways branch depending on the operands? Shared structure doesn’t necessarily mean there’s one clean, symbolic addition algorithm. You can have several overlapping strategies contributing to the answer.

The qualification is that a graph for one prompt shows a particular execution, and the replacement model is an approximation. Shared weights let us connect observations across examples, but establishing that a pathway actually performs the computation still calls for interventions and testing across inputs.

r001.rationale: It contrasts shared weights and connections across prompts with a graph showing the particular execution for one prompt.

r002.rationale: It states that two addition problems can activate different features while using overlapping computational pathways.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that a circuit traced on one addition problem gives you a local view: these are the features and connections that mattered for this particular input. The global weights let you ask whether those connections reflect a reusable mechanism across many inputs.

For addition, that means looking for shared structure in how the model represents numbers, combines them, and handles things like carries. Different problems can activate different features while still using overlapping computational pathways. So you shouldn’t imagine a completely separate circuit for every pair of numbers, or necessarily one clean, symbolic addition algorithm. You can have several strategies that share intermediate representations and contribute to the same answer.

The important distinction is between observing that the model got a sum right and identifying a mechanism that explains its behavior across a family of sums. The global analysis helps connect those individual traces, while interventions are what let you test whether the proposed shared structure is actually doing the work.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a single traced addition problem as a local view with global weights used to assess reusable connections across many inputs.

r002.rationale: It says different addition problems can activate different features while sharing overlapping computational pathways.
